Report 3: Descriptive Statistics and First Interpretations

Purdue AdmissionsAnalytics Dataset · Activity-Level Semantic Parsing · 2026-05-21
This report documents the first detailed descriptive analysis of the matched Purdue applicant dataset. The purpose is exploratory: to understand the structure of the applicant pool, inspect semantic feature behavior, and develop interpretable hypotheses before advancing to more sophisticated modeling.

1. Dataset Context

The current Purdue dataset combines parsed application features with real admissions outcomes. The matching process linked Purdue PDF-derived applicant records to an admissions-status database built from the master spreadsheet.

109matched Purdue applicants
80accepted or alternate-campus accepted
29rejected
997parsed activity blocks

This is not a random sample of all Purdue applicants. It is a consultant-mediated, selective, STEM-heavy population. Consequently, high GPA, strong coursework, and substantial extracurricular activity are already common. The most interesting signal is likely to appear in the semantic structure of applicants rather than in broad academic metrics alone.

2. Core Question: What Does the Activity Section Actually Measure?

A first hypothesis was that the number of activities might help distinguish admitted from rejected applicants. The activity-block parser showed that this is probably too crude. Most applicants report roughly the same number of activities, with a median near ten. That suggests raw activity count is partly shaped by the application platform and by coaching behavior.

The better question is not simply, “How many activities did the applicant list?” The better question is, “What kind of applicant structure do these activities reveal?”

3. Activity Category Composition

This graphic compares the proportion of activity blocks belonging to each category for accepted and rejected applicants. The horizontal axis gives the share of activity blocks in a category, not the number of students. The color separates the admitted and rejected groups.

Figure 1. Activity category composition by decision group. Categories such as Community Service, Computer/Technology, Robotics, Career-Oriented activity, Athletics, and Research begin to reveal the semantic profile of the applicant pool.

The key point is that activity categories are not evenly distributed across decisions. Accepted applicants show stronger representation in several applied or outward-facing areas, especially community service, computer/technology, robotics, and career-oriented activities. This does not prove causation. Rather, it suggests that admitted applicants more often occupy semantically rich regions of the activity space: technical construction, public contribution, and applied project engagement.

The result also helps explain why raw activity count is inadequate. Two applicants may each list ten activities, but one profile may be highly coherent around engineering, service, and technical construction, while another may be more diffuse or less aligned with the major.

4. Semantic Feature Means

The semantic feature extractor counts interpretable signals across the applicant record. These include leadership, research, CS/AI, service, prestige indicators, entrepreneurship, STEM signal, public contribution, and builder signal.

Figure 2. Mean semantic feature values for accepted and rejected applicants. The most visually important gaps appear in public contribution, STEM signal, builder signal, service, and CS/AI features.

This graphic is one of the strongest pieces of evidence that the semantic layer is meaningful. Accepted applicants tend to have higher values on several interpretable feature families. In particular, public contribution and STEM signal separate the groups more clearly than raw activity count did.

Public contribution combines leadership and service-related evidence. It may reflect students who do not merely participate, but organize, lead, teach, build communities, or serve identifiable groups.

STEM signal captures technical and research-oriented structure. In a Purdue-heavy dataset, this is naturally important, especially because the matched population includes many CS, engineering, data science, and biology applicants.

Builder signal is especially interesting. It is intended to approximate the applicant who makes things: programs, robots, startups, technical systems, engineering artifacts, or real-world projects. This may become one of the most useful conceptual features in the project.

5. Activity-Level Semantic Flag Rates

The previous graph works at the applicant-document level. This graph works at the activity-block level. It asks: among all parsed activities in a group, what proportion contain a particular semantic signal?

Figure 3. Activity-level semantic flag rates. This reduces some of the inflation that comes from counting repeated terms across an entire document.

This graphic is operationally valuable because it is easier to explain. Instead of saying an applicant had many keyword mentions, we can say that a larger share of accepted applicants’ activities contained CS/AI, service, or leadership signals.

The CS/AI separation is particularly notable. It appears in the category composition graph, the semantic means graph, and the flag-rate graph. When a pattern appears under several different representations, it becomes more credible as a genuine structural feature of the dataset.

Research, however, is more complicated. It does not separate the groups as strongly as expected. This may mean that research is now common among elite applicants, that research quality matters more than the number of references, or that research-heavy applicants are applying to especially competitive majors.

6. Estimated Annual Activity Hours

This graphic estimates commitment intensity by multiplying reported hours per week by weeks per year for each parsed activity. The figure compares the distributions of estimated annual activity hours by decision group.

Figure 4. Estimated annual activity hours by decision group. Accepted applicants appear slightly shifted upward, but the distributions overlap substantially.

The correct interpretation is nuanced. Activity intensity appears to matter somewhat, but it is not decisive by itself. There is heavy overlap between accepted and rejected applicants. This suggests that the number of hours alone cannot explain admissions outcomes.

In practical terms, this means that “more time spent” is not the same as “stronger applicant structure.” A student may spend many hours in an activity that has limited relevance to major fit or applicant narrative. Another student may spend fewer hours in a highly coherent technical or leadership activity that better reveals institutional fit.

7. Applicant Semantic Geometry

This scatterplot is the most conceptually important visualization so far. Each point represents an applicant. The horizontal axis measures STEM signal. The vertical axis measures public contribution signal. The color indicates admission outcome.

Figure 5. Applicant semantic geometry: STEM signal versus public contribution. The plot suggests that admissions may be better understood through multidimensional regions rather than a single scalar ranking.

The rejected applicants appear more concentrated in lower-signal regions, while admitted applicants extend into higher-STEM, higher-public-contribution, and hybrid regions. This is not a perfect separation, and it should not be treated as a deterministic rule. But it does suggest that applicant strength may be geometric rather than linear.

In other words, there may not be one single “best” applicant type. Some successful applicants may be highly technical. Others may be service-heavy leaders. Others may be builders, artists, athletes, or hybrid profiles. This supports the idea that admissions operates partly like a frontier problem: applicants can be strong in different directions.

8. First Modeling Context

A first semantic logistic model, Model V2, was also run. It achieved an ROC AUC of approximately 0.67 on a small test split. That is reasonable for a first-generation model with 109 matched applicants, noisy extracted features, class imbalance, and no serious course-rigor or essay-quality extraction yet.

The more important point is that semantic features changed the model geometry. SAT and GPA remained strong, but CS/AI, activity-block structure, service, athletics, and builder-related features also entered meaningfully. This suggests that the semantic layer is not merely decorative; it contributes structure beyond basic academic indicators.

The model should not be interpreted as a final admissions predictor. It is an infrastructure and signal-discovery model. The coefficient signs should also be interpreted cautiously because many semantic features are correlated with one another.

9. Important Cautions

Small sample size. The matched dataset currently contains only 109 applicants. This makes coefficients and performance metrics unstable.

Class imbalance. The matched sample contains many more accepted applicants than rejected applicants. A model can appear superficially successful by over-predicting admission.

Consultant-mediated selection. These students are not representative of the general Purdue applicant pool. The analysis describes this particular population.

Semantic extraction is still early. The current extractor is interpretable and useful, but it still overcounts some signals and requires normalization at the activity-block level.

Correlation is not causation. The graphs show association, not admissions policy.

10. Main Conclusion

The strongest finding so far is that applicant signal does not appear to reside primarily in the number of activities. The stronger signal appears to emerge from the semantic geometry of those activities: technical orientation, builder behavior, service, leadership, public contribution, activity intensity, and the alignment of those features with the applicant’s intended field.

This means the AdmissionsAnalytics project is moving from scalar applicant metrics toward structured applicant representation. That shift is the major conceptual achievement of this stage.

11. Next Steps

The next high-value steps are to stabilize the activity parser, normalize activity-level semantic features, separate role from organization, extract course-rigor features, and build major-specific models. The false-positive and false-negative cases from Model V2 should also be studied carefully because they may reveal omitted variables such as major competitiveness, essay quality, or institutional fit.
